questions.stem: What is the midpoint of the class interval $20 \leq x < 30$?
Why is the mean from grouped data called an 'estimate'?

options.text: Because grouped data is always unreliable
Because we use midpoints instead of the actual data values, which are unknown

questions.explanation: When data is grouped, the individual values are lost. We use the midpoint of each class as a representative value, which only gives an estimate.

questions.stem: A grouped frequency table has classes $0 \leq h < 10$ (freq 5), $10 \leq h < 20$ (freq 12), $20 \leq h < 30$ (freq 8). What is $\sum fx$?
The estimated mean from grouped data must lie:

options.text: At the midpoint of the modal class
Within the range of the data

questions.explanation: The estimated mean must lie within the range of the data (between the lowest and highest class boundaries). If it does not, there is an error.

questions.stem: When calculating the estimated mean, you should divide $\sum fx$ by:
questions.explanation: Estimated mean $= \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$, where $\sum f$ is the total frequency (the total number of data items).

questions.stem: A table has unequal class widths: $0 \leq x < 5$, $5 \leq x < 15$, $15 \leq x < 30$. Can you still estimate the mean?

options.text: Yes, the midpoint method works regardless of class width
Only if you use frequency density instead
Only if you make the class widths equal first
No, the method only works with equal class widths

questions.explanation: The estimated mean formula works for both equal and unequal class widths. You simply find the midpoint of each class and use $\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$.

questions.stem: A common error is using the lower boundary instead of the midpoint. If the class is $10 \leq x < 20$ with frequency 15, the correct $fx$ value is:
questions.explanation: The midpoint of $10 \leq x < 20$ is $\frac{10+20}{2} = 15$. So $fx = 15 \times 15 = 225$.
